title: Spot the reliability problem
brief:
Two trained abstractors independently reviewed the same 10 patient records for a hand-hygiene compliance audit. Their results for 5 of the records are shown below. For each record, decide whether the pair's results indicate a **reliability problem** or **no reliability problem**.

Reliability problem = the two abstractors reached different conclusions on whether the criterion was met, was not met, or was uncodeable.

items.label: Record #1 — Abstractor A: Met · Abstractor B: Met
Record #2 — Abstractor A: Not met · Abstractor B: Exclude (missing data)
Record #3 — Abstractor A: Met · Abstractor B: Not met
Record #4 — Abstractor A: Exclude · Abstractor B: Exclude
Record #5 — Abstractor A: Not met · Abstractor B: Not met

debrief.correct: Correct. Records #1, #4, and #5 show agreement between abstractors — same conclusion, no problem. Records #2 and #3 show disagreement. Record #2 is a subtle case: 'Not met' and 'Exclude' are different conclusions. One abstractor decided the criterion was failed; the other decided there was not enough data to judge. These require adjudication — a senior reviewer or a third abstractor must resolve the discrepancy before the data can be used.
debrief.wrong: Agreement means both abstractors reached the same conclusion — 'Met/Met', 'Not met/Not met', or 'Exclude/Exclude'. Any mix of different codes is a reliability problem, even when the codes are 'similar' (like 'Not met' vs 'Exclude'). Record #2 is the hardest: 'Not met' and 'Exclude' sound like near-agreement, but they carry different implications for the measure rate and the improvement response. Always treat different codes as a reliability flag.
debrief.rule_cited: Inter-rater reliability — chart abstraction training and adjudication. NAHQ HQ Essentials.
